title: Judges 2:11–23
context: The narrator now states the pattern that will govern the book. The children of Israel did evil in the LORD’s sight and served the Baals. They abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of Egypt, followed the gods of the surrounding peoples, bowed down to them, and provoked the LORD to anger. They served Baal and the Ashtaroth. The LORD’s anger burned; he delivered them to raiders, sold them into the hands of their enemies, and they could no longer stand. Wherever they went out, his hand was against them for evil, as he had spoken and sworn, and they were very distressed. The LORD raised up judges, who saved them, yet they did not listen to the judges and quickly turned to other gods. When he raised a judge, he was with the judge and saved them all the days of that judge, for it grieved the LORD because of their groaning under oppression; but when the judge died, they turned back and dealt more corruptly than their fathers, and they did not give up their stubborn ways. Because the nation transgressed his covenant and did not listen to his voice, the LORD says he will no longer drive out the nations Joshua left, that by them he may test Israel, to see if they will keep his way as their fathers kept it, or not. So he left those nations, without driving them out hastily, and he did not deliver them into Joshua’s hand. Both traditions read this cycle as shared ground: sin, anger, oppression, distress, a raised deliverer, temporary salvation, and relapse. The testing of verses 20–23 belongs with that same ground. God leaves the nations in his providence in order to test Israel. Classical Arminians affirm exhaustive foreknowledge, so the testing language is not a claim that God is ignorant of the outcome; the test is still a real probation of Israel’s walk. Reformed readers hear the same purpose as God’s counsel to disclose and to deal with the people. Neither reading should be forced into a fork over testing or providence.

verses.text: The children of Israel did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and served the Baals.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Israel “did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and served the Baals.” The cycle opens with evil as the LORD sees it, and with service to the Baals.

Arminian readers hear a real turning. The people actually serve other gods; the evil is measured in the LORD’s sight, not in their own, and they are accountable for it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same standard and the same service. Evil is defined by the LORD’s sight, and the Baals—the local lords of the land—are already named as the rival to whom they give themselves.

Both traditions take the verse as the first stroke of the pattern, shared ground of apostasy, without a contrast over the details of Canaanite religion.

verses.text: They abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and followed other gods, of the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed themselves down to them; and they provoked the LORD to anger.
verses.arminianNotes:
They abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, followed other gods of the peoples around them, bowed themselves down to them, and provoked the LORD to anger.

Arminian readers hear abandonment of the redeemer, not a slight lapse. The God they leave is the one who brought them out of Egypt; they bow to the neighbors’ gods and provoke his anger by a genuine turning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same betrayal of the exodus God, and the bowing down that provokes his anger. The surrounding peoples’ gods are not an enrichment of Israel’s worship; they are the object of a forsaking.

Both traditions read the verse as covenant apostasy that kindles real anger, shared ground at the heart of the cycle.

verses.text: They abandoned the LORD, and served Baal and the Ashtaroth.
verses.arminianNotes:
They abandoned the LORD, and served Baal and the Ashtaroth. The forsaking of verse 12 is now named again, with Baal and the Ashtaroth paired as the cult they served.

Arminian readers hear how complete the turn is. They do not merely add a name; they serve Baal and the Ashtaroth, and they have abandoned the LORD to do it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the pairing as a fuller report of the service already mentioned. The male and female cults of the land receive what belongs to the LORD.

Both traditions read the verse as a second, sharper statement of the same apostasy, without forcing a contrast over the history of those cults.

verses.text: The LORD’s anger burned against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of raiders who plundered them. He sold them into the hands of their enemies all around, so that they could no longer stand before their enemies.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s anger burned against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of raiders who plundered them. He sold them into the hands of their enemies all around, so that they could no longer stand before their enemies.

Arminian readers hear a real judgment that answers a real abandonment. God delivers and sells; they cannot stand. The anger is judicial, and the distress is earned by the forsaking just described.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the burning anger, the delivering, and the selling are all the LORD’s acts. The people can no longer stand because he has handed them over, in keeping with his covenant warnings.

Both traditions take the verse as God’s own judgment, shared ground, not as a contrast over whether the anger is true. It is the LORD’s opposition to their evil.

verses.text: Wherever they went out, the LORD’s hand was against them for evil, as the LORD had spoken, and as the LORD had sworn to them; and they were very distressed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wherever they went out, the LORD’s hand was against them for evil, as the LORD had spoken, and as the LORD had sworn to them; and they were very distressed. The hand against them fulfills a word already spoken and sworn.

Arminian readers hear covenant warning come due. “for evil” here means for their calamity, not that God himself does moral wrong. They are very distressed under a hand they had been told would turn against them if they forsook him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the double clause “as the LORD had spoken, and as the LORD had sworn to them;” that distress is not an accident of history; it is the kept word of God, and his hand is against them wherever they go out.

Both traditions take “for evil” as harm or calamity in judgment, and they take the distress as the fruit of that sworn word, shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.” Salvation begins with God’s raising, and the judges really save.

Arminian readers hear mercy that meets distress with a real deliverer. God raises judges; they save the people; Israel is actually rescued and given a living chance to return to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the LORD is the one who raised up the judges and that the saving is theirs only as his means. The people do not first reform and then receive a judge; he raises and saves out of the plunderers’ hand.

Both traditions take the verse as grace in the cycle, shared ground: deliverance is God’s initiative, and it is a true salvation for its time.

verses.text: Yet they didn’t listen to their judges; for they prostituted themselves to other gods, and bowed themselves down to them. They quickly turned away from the way in which their fathers walked, obeying the LORD’s commandments. They didn’t do so.
verses.arminianNotes:
Yet they didn’t listen to their judges; they prostituted themselves to other gods and bowed themselves down to them. They quickly turned away from the way in which their fathers walked, obeying the LORD’s commandments. They didn’t do so.

Arminian readers hear a real refusal to listen, even when judges stand among them. The prostitution is covenant unfaithfulness; they turn quickly from the fathers’ obedient way, and they are to blame for it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the “Yet” as the tragedy inside the deliverance. Raised judges do not automatically produce a listening people. The fathers’ way of obeying the LORD’s commandments is left, and left quickly.

Both traditions read the verse as unfaithfulness during the judges’ own days, shared ground, not only after the judges die.

verses.text: When the LORD raised up judges for them, then the LORD was with the judge, and saved them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge; for it grieved the LORD because of their groaning by reason of those who oppressed them and troubled them.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the LORD raised up judges for them, the LORD was with the judge, and saved them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge; for it grieved the LORD because of their groaning by reason of those who oppressed them and troubled them.

Arminian readers hear both presence and compassion. God is with the judge and saves all that judge’s days, and he is truly grieved by their groaning. The mercy is not reluctant theater; their cry moves him to save.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the LORD’s being with the judge is the reason the salvation lasts all the days of the judge, and that the grief named here is the LORD’s own compassion toward a groaning people. The cycle’s rescue is rooted in that grief, not in Israel’s merit.

Both traditions take the grief as true mercy, shared ground, without opening a side debate about divine impassibility as if it were the point of this verse.

verses.text: But when the judge was dead, they turned back, and dealt more corruptly than their fathers in following other gods to serve them and to bow down to them. They didn’t cease what they were doing, or give up their stubborn ways.
verses.arminianNotes:
But when the judge was dead, they turned back, and dealt more corruptly than their fathers in following other gods to serve them and to bow down to them. They didn’t cease what they were doing, or give up their stubborn ways.

Arminian readers hear a downward spiral that is chosen again at each death. The deliverance of the judge’s days does not remake the people; they turn back, grow worse than their fathers, and will not give up stubborn ways.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the death of the judge as the unveiling of what the people still are. They turn back and deal more corruptly; the stubborn ways are not surrendered. Temporary salvation does not, by itself, create lasting covenant loyalty.

Both traditions read the verse as the relapse that completes the cycle and deepens it, shared ground for the books that follow in this pattern.

verses.text: The LORD’s anger burned against Israel; and he said, “Because this nation transgressed my covenant which I commanded their fathers, and has not listened to my voice,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s anger burned against Israel, and he said, “Because this nation transgressed my covenant which I commanded their fathers, and has not listened to my voice,” grounding the words that follow in covenant breach and in a refusal to listen.

Arminian readers hear a just cause named before the sentence of verses 21–22. This nation has transgressed what God commanded the fathers, and has not listened; the test that follows is not an arbitrary experiment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same ground: anger, transgression of the commanded covenant, and a voice not listened to. What God will do with the nations Joshua left is an answer to that breach, not a change of purpose detached from Israel’s sin.

Both traditions take the verse as the stated reason for the decision that follows, shared ground at the opening of the speech.

verses.text: I also will no longer drive out any of the nations that Joshua left when he died from before them;
verses.arminianNotes:
The speech continues: “I also will no longer drive out any of the nations that Joshua left when he died from before them;” so God now says he will not complete the dispossession of what Joshua left.

Arminian readers hear this as the divine side of chapter 1’s unfinished map. Israel would not finish the work; God now says he also will no longer drive those nations out. Both the failure and this word are real.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the “I also” and the nations “that Joshua left when he died”. The leftover peoples stand under God’s decision as well as under Israel’s history. Chapter 1’s lists and this sentence are to be held together, not played against each other.

Both traditions read the verse as God’s settled refusal to finish that driving out, shared ground with verse 3, not a fork that would make only one of those explanations count.

verses.text: that by them I may test Israel, to see if they will keep the LORD’s way to walk therein, as their fathers kept it, or not.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The purpose is given: “that by them I may test Israel, to see if they will keep the LORD’s way to walk therein, as their fathers kept it, or not.” The leftover nations become a test of Israel’s walk.

Arminian readers hear a genuine probation. The test is not empty; Israel really must keep the LORD’s way, or not, as the fathers did. Classical Arminianism affirms God’s exhaustive foreknowledge, so “to see if” does not mean that God is waiting to learn an unknown future. It is the language of a real test that engages their responsible will.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same purpose as God’s counsel. He leaves the nations in order to test Israel, and “to see if” is the accommodated language of a test that will manifest whether they walk in the LORD’s way. Providence governs the leaving; the test is a true means of disclosure and of dealing with the people, not an open future.

Both traditions take testing and providence as shared ground here. Neither reading is open theism, and the verse should not be forced into an Arminian–Reformed fork.

verses.text: So the LORD left those nations, without driving them out hastily. He didn’t deliver them into Joshua’s hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
So the LORD left those nations, without driving them out hastily. “He didn’t deliver them into Joshua’s hand.” The narrator now states the fact: God left them, he did not drive them out in haste, and he had not given them all into Joshua’s hand.

Arminian readers hear a purpose that reaches back into Joshua’s days as well as forward into the judges’. The unfinished conquest is not only Israel’s delay; the LORD did not deliver those nations hastily into Joshua’s hand, and Israel must still walk faithfully among what was left.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same summary as God’s own act. He left the nations; he did not drive them out hastily; he did not deliver them into Joshua’s hand. Verses 20–22 have given the reason: covenant transgression and a test of Israel’s way.

Both traditions hold together Israel’s failure, the LORD’s judicial word, and his testing purpose. The close of the chapter is shared ground, not a contrast that would set those truths against one another.
